:::{#exm-exponential-decay}
#### The same factor over two run lengths

Take $\iterpoint{\steplen}{0} = 0.1$ and $\decay = 0.99$.
The [step length](#def-exponential-decay) at $t = 1000$ and at $t = 100000$ is:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### R

```{r}
#| label: exponential-decay-r
#| code-fold: false
s0_ed <- 0.1
decay_ed <- 0.99
t_ed <- c(1000, 100000)
step_ed <- s0_ed * decay_ed^t_ed
tibble::tibble(t = t_ed, step_length = step_ed)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: exponential-decay-python
#| code-fold: false
s0_ed, decay_ed = 0.1, 0.99
for t_ed in [1000, 100000]:
    print(t_ed, s0_ed * decay_ed ** t_ed);
```

:::

At $t = 1000$ the step length is about $4.3 \times 10^{-6}$. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
At $t = 100000$ it is $0$ in floating-point arithmetic.
One factor gives two very different schedules.

<!-- no-figure: the example tabulates two step lengths -->

:::
